profile.headline: I design brand, product, and 3D systems - and build the AI pipelines that produce them at scale.
profile.summary: This portfolio was designed and built with Figma Make, Codex, and Claude Code - driven by a custom prompt system that walks a phased roadmap, executing build and QA tasks in an iterative loop.

projects.title: Quiver
projects.category: Creative Direction / Generative Production / Motion Systems
projects.shortDescription: Four product launch films developed from a sparse brief: creative direction, constrained generative production, motion design, editing, AI-generated music and reusable production tooling.
projects.fullDescription: Four launch films for Quiver, a partner team UNCX worked with, made from a sparse brief. I took it on as a client through that relationship and handled everything from script and art direction to local AI generation, motion, edit and audio.
projects.role: Creative direction, script, AI imagery and footage, motion, edit and audio

overlaySections.title: Context and role
overlaySections.body: Quiver was a separate team that UNCX partnered with, not part of UNCX. The brief came through that relationship: make a marketing video from a logo, the existing product and a rough ident reference. There was no film treatment. I owned the concept, script, art direction, generation workflow, motion design, edit, audio and production tooling.

overlaySections.title: Problem
overlaySections.body: The film had to feel like one intentional world across generated footage, product messages, motion graphics and music. The main technical risks were reliability: the bowstring had to make physical sense between frames, and the model kept introducing a face on a character that was meant to stay hidden.

overlaySections.title: Constraints
overlaySections.body:
- A sparse brief: a logo, the product and a rough ident reference
- Many scenes and images, each needing several attempts to get one correct result
- Cloud generation made that volume of attempts too costly on subscription services
- Local inference on one RTX 4090, with the preparation and storage that brings
- Product messages had to stay legible over dark, atmospheric footage

overlaySections.title: Key decisions
overlaySections.body:
- Generate locally: with Wan 2.2 in ComfyUI on my own RTX 4090, the main cost became time rather than money, so I could render 3 to 5 attempts per scene and keep the one that looked right
- Keep the job simple for the model: the black-and-white style and rendering individual elements separately meant each generation was tightly controlled rather than complex
- Design the shots around the model: planned start and end frames kept the action legible and avoided transitions that invite impossible bowstring physics
- Run the pipeline with agents: Claude controlled ComfyUI to queue a variety of scenes while Codex generated the source images in the same project folder
- Composite rather than bake in: the generated footage, mist and effects stayed as separate layers in After Effects, with typography and product layers authored on top, so timing and readability were controlled in the edit
- Build tooling, not one film: AI-assisted scripts created scene comps, text precomps, impact markers and shared 2.5D depth, so four edits came from one system

overlaySections.title: Compromises
overlaySections.body:
- Time instead of money: every scene took several local renders to get one usable result
- Retries for details that were easy to overlook, such as finger position and depth ordering, for example a bowstring starting on one side of a hand and ending on the other because the source images were set up wrong

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: Four finished 16:9 films at 1920 x 1080 and 24 fps: a 42-second basic and a 58-second advanced explanation, each with and without phone imagery, plus a structured footage library and a reusable After Effects production system. The work is approved for public portfolio use. No campaign reach, conversion or commercial figures are claimed.

overlaySections.title: What I learned
overlaySections.body: Where the limits of reliable output sit. Keeping the model's job small and controlled, one element at a time in a black-and-white style, made generation dependable; the failures that remained were specific and predictable, mainly bowstring logic and unwanted faces, so they could be caught and re-rendered.

projects.title: Solana Diary
projects.shortDescription: An automated Solana-media pipeline for X: seven services that turned live on-chain data and news into designed, on-brand posts - each one approved by me from Telegram before it published, all running on free-tier APIs.

I built the system and designed every asset: seven services that turned live on-chain data and news into on-brand posts for X, each approved by me from Telegram before it published.

projects.role: Solo build - brand, design system & engineering

overlaySections.title: Context and role
overlaySections.body: Solana Diary was a UNCX partner project aiming to gain traction in Solana marketing on X. The name and intent were established before I came on board. My role was to build the code and graphics systems and design all of the assets: the identity, the post templates, the backend and the approval flow.

overlaySections.title: Problem
overlaySections.body: Daily crypto content is a production line: fresh data every few hours, constant news, and a hard requirement that nothing misleading or unsafe goes out. Manual production does not scale; full automation risks posting bad data or promoting a token about to rug.

overlaySections.title: Constraints
overlaySections.body:
- Free-tier APIs only, with no budget for paid data
- Every post had to be safe to publish, with one accountable person signing off
- The name and positioning were fixed before I joined
- X as the single distribution channel

overlaySections.title: Key decisions
overlaySections.body:
- Keep a human veto on every post: the system gathered, rendered and drafted, and publishing waited for a tap or a reply-to edit in Telegram. One misleading post is worse than any amount of manual effort.
- Graphics from code, not AI: every post was rendered from my Figma templates populated with live data, so output stayed on-brand and factual.
- Choose APIs by limit type: providers with per-second rather than monthly limits, plus a rate-limiter pacing every call, made all-day data possible with no paid plan.
- Make news volume controllable: a daily limit on automated news attempts could be raised on days with weak data and lowered on busy posting days, and approved news could be scheduled.

overlaySections.title: Compromises
overlaySections.body:
- Human approval on every post capped throughput in exchange for safety
- The magazine-style web front end was paused: rebuilding it during the backend rewrite would have been wasted work, and the plan was to bring it back once the new backend was in place
- The name was outside my control, and it is what got the account banned

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: The pipeline ran daily as designed: seven Railway services, a rate-limited data layer, a code-driven rendering engine, a Telegram approval flow and a template system of roughly fifteen post families. X then permanently suspended the account for "impersonation" because the name was too close to an established brand, and did not reinstate it.

overlaySections.title: What I learned
overlaySections.body: Platform risk is a design constraint from day one. When you automate publishing, the identity you publish under needs the same scrutiny as the code.

projects.title: UNCX Unified Menu
projects.shortDescription: Cross-product navigation component system with variable-driven Figma prototypes, research-backed hierarchy, and scalable state logic.
projects.fullDescription: One navigation system for every UNCX Network product. I researched the patterns, set the hierarchy and delivered a variable-driven Figma component that was signed off and built.

overlaySections.title: Context and role
overlaySections.body: In-house at UNCX Network, where each product had grown its own menu, so users moving between EVM tools, Solana products, the Academy and the homepage met a different structure every time. I owned the research, hierarchy, component design and implementation specification.

overlaySections.title: Problem
overlaySections.body: Replace inconsistent per-product menus with one system that stays efficient and navigable across many products and sub-brands.

overlaySections.title: Constraints
overlaySections.body:
- Many products and sub-brands had to fit one menu structure
- Highly specialised products: the menu had to explain what each one does without slowing down experienced users
- Some products earn far more than others and needed priority without devaluing the rest

overlaySections.title: Key decisions
overlaySections.body:
- Set definitive levels of hierarchy, with the revenue-generating products given visual priority
- Make the menu mildly educational: short descriptions so newcomers learn the ecosystem while experts scan past them
- Build it as a variable-driven component with configurable content slots, so each product context uses the same system

overlaySections.title: Compromises
overlaySections.body:
- Non-value-generating menu options were de-prioritised to keep the structure efficient
- UNCX is a developer-led product organisation, so the design continued to evolve in implementation; the mobile version in particular has since been adapted by the development team

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: The design was signed off and implemented across the product suite. Elements have since been refined by the development team as the products changed, with the core hierarchy and structure intact.

overlaySections.title: What I learned
overlaySections.body: Navigation hierarchy is a business decision as much as a UX one. In a fast-moving, developer-led team, the most durable part of a design is the structure and reasoning behind it, so that is what needs to be clearest in the handoff.

projects.title: UNCX Company Rebrand
projects.shortDescription: The rebrand of Unicrypt Network into UNCX Network: a logo, brand, marketing and website rebuild in 2022, then a more modern brand, website and Academy in 2024, directed by me with an outside studio and finished in-house.
projects.fullDescription: The rebrand of Unicrypt Network into UNCX Network, in two phases. In 2022 I rebuilt the logo, brand, marketing and website myself; in 2024 an outside studio worked from my direction on a more modern system, and I completed it in-house.

media.alt: The Unicrypt Network brand before the 2022 rebrand

overlaySections.title: Context and role
overlaySections.body: In-house at UNCX Network, formerly Unicrypt Network. In 2022 I designed the new logo, brand, marketing and website, with a developer implementing the site. In 2024 I directed an outside studio on a branding, marketing and website update, which also introduced the Academy, then finished the website, Academy and brand rollout in-house.

overlaySections.title: Problem
overlaySections.body: The brand had to move from Unicrypt to UNCX, then mature: different visual treatments per product, no systemised colour or typography, and marketing that did not match the product UI.

overlaySections.title: Constraints
overlaySections.body:
- 2022: a short-notice name change with minimal runway
- 2024: an outside studio without deep knowledge of the brand or products
- The website, the new Academy and the brand rollout all had to land together
- Several development subteams had to implement the designs consistently

overlaySections.title: Key decisions
overlaySections.body:
- 2022: rebuild the logo, brand, marketing and website myself, with a developer handling implementation, to move quickly
- 2024: set the direction for a less technical, more modern style, with new fonts, wider bold type and an abstract visual system, and have an outside studio build it
- Bring the unfinished work back in-house: I completed the website, Academy and brand designs, a developer built the sites, and I added imagery, designed extra pages and tidied the copy

overlaySections.title: Compromises
overlaySections.body:
- The 2022 change favoured speed over a complete system, which the 2024 phase delivered
- Finishing the studio work in-house added to my own workload
- Consistent implementation across subteams took longer than the design itself

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: A brand that moved from Unicrypt to UNCX Network, then to a modern system across the website, Academy and marketing: guidelines, Figma component libraries, 10+ website page designs, marketing templates and motion style references.

overlaySections.title: What I learned
overlaySections.body: Scope a studio engagement to a finished deliverable. Studios tend to extend the work rather than close it, and they do not always research the product; waiting on them for copy they could draft themselves stalls a project, so owning the content and the finish in-house was faster.

projects.title: Badger Club App
projects.shortDescription: Full-stack badge tracking platform with dark/light themes, role-based dashboards, Supabase backend, and Resend email integration.
projects.fullDescription: A badge-tracking app for group leaders that I am designing and building solo. Leaders manage progress and messages; families see progress and contact the leader without an account.

overlaySections.title: Context and role
overlaySections.body: A personal product, designed and built end to end: product design, React frontend, Supabase data model, Google authentication, Resend email and Cloudflare security, using AI-assisted development tools.

overlaySections.title: Problem
overlaySections.body: Badge tracking relied on spreadsheets, paper records and inconsistent communication between leaders and parents, with leaders carrying the whole admin burden.

overlaySections.title: Constraints
overlaySections.body:
- Legal and complexity limits on accounts for parents and children
- Messaging across a leader inbox, leader email and parent email added significant complexity
- A solo build, so scope had to stay controllable

overlaySections.title: Key decisions
overlaySections.body:
- Leader-only accounts: parents and children see progress through shareable links with no sign-up
- Split messaging by audience: leaders use an in-app inbox with email notifications; parents receive messages by email
- Scope the build as atomised phases so AI-assisted development did not drift

overlaySections.title: Compromises
overlaySections.body:
- The original multi-user platform, with accounts for leaders, parents and children, was dropped
- A fully mirrored inbox was simplified to reduce Resend complexity

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: An earlier version was shown to real users through a contact, with positive responses and clear direction on design improvements. The whole system has since been redesigned and updated, and I am now building the legal and EU regulatory requirements needed before launch.

overlaySections.title: What I learned
overlaySections.body: Removing accounts was the strongest product decision: fewer barriers for families mattered more than more features. The project also sharpened my development process, and its rules and guidance now feed my AI product template for new builds.

projects.title: UNCX Video & 3D System
projects.shortDescription: End-to-end video production pipeline spanning Cinema 4D, After Effects, and Redshift - built for repeatable, high-frequency output.
projects.fullDescription: A modular video production system for UNCX Network, built so launches, explainers, tutorials and partner content could ship from one asset library, and now being rebuilt as an automated pipeline in code.

overlaySections.title: Context and role
overlaySections.body: In-house at UNCX Network. Production had been fragmented across freelancers and one-off files. I designed and ran the whole pipeline alongside other responsibilities.

overlaySections.title: Problem
overlaySections.body: No shared asset library, no consistent motion language and no templates, so every video started from zero.

overlaySections.title: Constraints
overlaySections.body:
- Time: one person running the full production alongside other work
- Long scripts from the marketing team and tight delivery timelines
- Many formats, from short launch trailers to long-form Academy content

overlaySections.title: Key decisions
overlaySections.body:
- Introduce script length limits to keep videos deliverable
- Replace per-scene custom animation with categorised, reusable templates
- Build reusable Cinema 4D scenes, camera rigs and Redshift materials so a new product could enter an established visual world
- Rebuild the pipeline in code: video generation, text inputs and voiceover are automated with ElevenLabs, Remotion and Blender, with the system queuing the 3D work it needs

overlaySections.title: Compromises
overlaySections.body:
- Fewer unique scenes per video in exchange for speed and consistency
- Unnecessary scenes were stripped back from early, over-scoped productions
- 3D is the last part of the automated pipeline and still in progress: AI tools are not yet reliable for it, so the plan is to model manually in Blender while the system handles the rest

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: A production system of Cinema 4D scene templates, After Effects project structures, Redshift material libraries and thumbnail templates, used for 200+ videos at UNCX Network, including event films such as EthCC 2025 and Avalanche Summit. Its successor automates generation, text and voiceover, with 3D in progress.

overlaySections.title: What I learned
overlaySections.body: Manual 3D design, finding visual analogies for every line of script, is mentally exhausting; on top of building the motion graphics and my other duties, it led to creative burnout. Automating everything around the 3D, and choosing between template libraries, existing assets and 3D generation tools, taught me to spend my creative energy only where it is needed.

projects.title: UNCX Academy Brand & Platform
projects.shortDescription: Educational platform brand and design system - logotype, component library, article system, video pages, and glossary for DeFi learning.
projects.fullDescription: The brand and platform design for UNCX Academy, a DeFi education site. I wrote the brief, an external team built the foundations, and I completed the designs in-house, with my video system feeding its learning library.

overlaySections.title: Context and role
overlaySections.body: In-house at UNCX Network. I wrote the brief and specification; an external team delivered the logotype, identity and component library; I completed the page designs, hero graphics and visuals, then handed finished designs to an in-house developer who built the site and CMS.

overlaySections.title: Problem
overlaySections.body: DeFi education was scattered across blog posts, YouTube and documentation, with no unified platform, visual language or learning structure.

overlaySections.title: Constraints
overlaySections.body:
- The external team lacked the product context for content-specific designs
- Several content types (articles, videos, glossary, integrations) each needed their own template and navigation
- The platform had to align with the parent UNCX brand

overlaySections.title: Key decisions
overlaySections.body:
- Apply a more structured handoff than on the rebrand: external team for foundations, in-house for content-specific design
- Give each content type its own page template within one component system
- Build the platform and the video content from the same brand specification so they fit together

overlaySections.title: Compromises
overlaySections.body:
- Content-specific design stayed in-house, adding to my workload
- The external team could not deliver the hero concepts I wanted, so the site launched with static images, with the intention that I would design them myself; time never allowed it

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: A complete Figma design system with page templates for Main, Articles, Videos, Glossary, Integrations and About, built and launched by an in-house developer. I still produce the article header banners for ongoing marketing output.

overlaySections.title: What I learned
overlaySections.body: Lessons from one external engagement carried straight into the next: the handoff process mattered as much as the design.

projects.title: Noticia Lingo App
projects.shortDescription: Language learning app with an AI-assisted classroom, real news articles, Google authentication, Supabase backend, and structured quiz flows.
projects.fullDescription: A language-learning app that turns real news into lessons, starting with English speakers learning Spanish. I am designing and building it solo, planning early for multiple languages, legal launch and scale.

media.alt: Learner dashboard: today's lessons, daily goal and streak
Comprehension exercise built from the article
Settings for reminder time, languages and learning level

overlaySections.title: Context and role
overlaySections.body: A personal product in development. I own the product design and the build: React, Supabase and Google authentication, with AI-assisted development tools.

overlaySections.title: Problem
overlaySections.body: Traditional language apps rely on decontextualised flashcards and drills, and learners lose motivation because the content feels disconnected from real usage.

overlaySections.title: Constraints
overlaySections.body:
- Lessons have to work against any news article, not fixed question-and-answer pairs
- Each language needs its own grammar and tooling
- Launching legally in the US and EU requires compliance work before launch
- Hosting costs need to stay low now and scale later

overlaySections.title: Key decisions
overlaySections.body:
- Build a multilingual framework from the start, but launch with English to Spanish: later languages then need only per-language grammar and tooling, not a rewrite
- Design lessons as reusable puzzle logic that works against any article
- Personalise difficulty with learning levels, and specify personalised news for premium membership
- Build the legal groundwork for a US and EU launch now, as with Badger Club
- Move the database from Supabase and Vercel to Neon, and potentially Cloudflare, to cut costs now and at scale

overlaySections.title: Compromises
overlaySections.body: - More complexity and time up front in exchange for a simpler path once there are real users

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: A working app with every lesson type built and working well, learning levels for personalised difficulty, and the multilingual and legal foundations in place. Personalised premium news is being specified and the database migration is under way.

overlaySections.title: What I learned
overlaySections.body: More planning and building now means fewer headaches later. Decisions that are cheap before launch, such as architecture, compliance and hosting, are expensive after it. Like Badger Club, this project feeds my AI product template.

projects.title: UNCX App Prototyping
projects.shortDescription: Rapid prototyping across token minting, launchpad flows, Telegram bots, NFT minting, and full launchpad concepts - from wireframes to interactive concepts.
projects.fullDescription: Five years of product concepts for UNCX Network: token minting, launchpads, Telegram bots and NFT tooling. Much of the value was deciding early whether a product was worth building at all.

overlaySections.title: Context and role
overlaySections.body: In-house at UNCX Network, 2021 to 2026. I produced route layouts, flow diagrams, wireframes and interactive Figma prototypes so features could be judged before development committed. Some became real products; others stopped at concept.

overlaySections.title: Problem
overlaySections.body: In a startup, a prototype is often not about perfecting the journey but about deciding whether a product is worth building, and developers otherwise built from text specifications that drifted from intent.

overlaySections.title: Constraints
overlaySections.body:
- Requirements arrived gradually as projects developed
- Novel DeFi processes with no established UX conventions to reference
- Every product had unique abilities, so UI could rarely be reused between them
- Development time had to go to the products most worth it

overlaySections.title: Key decisions
overlaySections.body:
- Start every project from the layout of its routes, then work out interactions in FigJam flow diagrams
- Show stakeholders the limits and depth of a system early, so they understood the build complexity and whether it was worth the time
- Use wireframing templates for sitemap and interaction planning, then start the real design system from the ground up, or from a fork, once the build was approved
- Keep a standard base of colours and fonts, but design the UI elements fresh for each product

overlaySections.title: Compromises
overlaySections.body:
- Many projects never started, because concepting showed they would take too much time for a small additional product
- Approved concepts often had to be rebuilt in a proper design system after the wireframe stage

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: Figma concepts across token minting, launchpads, Telegram bot and app flows, NFT minting and stealth launch admin. Some shipped as real products, others stopped at concept, and several were ruled out before development time was spent.

overlaySections.title: What I learned
overlaySections.body: Every project is different. Product design systems only become useful once you know you are building; before that, the job is to show stakeholders the real depth of the work so they can decide whether it is worth it, and accept that it may never leave the first stage.

projects.title: This Site: An Agentic Build System
projects.shortDescription: This portfolio is itself a case study - designed with Figma Make and built by a prompt system that walks a phased roadmap, executing build and QA tasks in an iterative loop.
projects.fullDescription: This site, built as its own case study: a phased roadmap executed by AI coding agents, with automated gates between steps and my review at each phase boundary.

overlaySections.title: Context and role
overlaySections.body: Self-initiated. I set the direction, wrote the roadmap and prompt system, and review every phase; Claude Code and Codex execute the build.

overlaySections.title: Problem
overlaySections.body: AI-assisted development fails in two familiar ways: drift, where the agent wanders off-spec during long builds, and erosion, where many small edits wear down the architecture.

overlaySections.title: Constraints
overlaySections.body:
- Agents need tightly scoped tasks to stay on-spec
- Every change has to be reviewable by one person
- The site has to be production quality, not a demo

overlaySections.title: Key decisions
overlaySections.body:
- Decompose the roadmap into phases, and phases into atomised tasks with acceptance criteria
- Gate each step with type checks, tests, lint and a production build
- Treat the roadmap as the source of truth: plan changes are explicit edits, never silent divergence
- Set up cross-project hooks and CI checks that enforce standards and workflow rules, not just describe them

overlaySections.title: Compromises
overlaySections.body:
- More planning time up front to prevent drift later
- Phase gates trade raw speed for reviewability

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: A production site built with React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind 4, a JSON content model, a rate-limited contact relay and a test suite, with a commit history that records the workflow.

overlaySections.title: What I learned
overlaySections.body: Written guidance is thorough but not enough on its own. For the most critical parts of development, such as writing up notes, adversarial tests and appropriate wording, hooks and CI checks are what guarantee correctness.
